The Great Reform Act of 1832. A watershed moment in British history when the aristocratic grip on Parliament was finally broken and the principle was established that representation should reflect population and economic power.

Before the Reform Act, Parliament was a monument to absurdity. Tiny villages with a handful of voters sent two MPs to Parliament while the industrial city of Manchester, with tens of thousands of people, sent none. These were the rotten boroughs, constituencies so small that a single landlord could essentially control them. The unreformed system had made sense in medieval England but was grotesque in an industrial age.

The Whig Prime Minister, Earl Grey, introduced a bill to reform Parliament in 1831. It was rejected. He introduced it again in 1832. It was rejected again. The resistance from Tory peers in the House of Lords was fierce. They understood that reform meant the end of their political monopoly. Finally, the King agreed to create enough new peers to break the Tory resistance. The Act passed.

The Reform Act eliminated fifty-six rotten boroughs entirely and drastically reduced representation from another thirty. Those seats were redistributed to growing industrial cities and urban areas. For the first time, Manchester and Birmingham would send MPs to Parliament.

The franchise was expanded, but only modestly. Before reform, roughly three percent of the adult male population could vote. After reform, roughly seven percent. Still, the working class was excluded entirely. So were all women. Property qualifications remained—voters had to own property above a certain value. Yet this was progress. The old system of aristocratic control had been breached. The principle was established: representation should reflect where people lived and the economic capacity they possessed.

Robert Peel and the Conservative Party initially opposed reform. They feared the chaos and the loss of their power. But they recognized that the choice before the country was between gradual reform or violent revolution. The memory of Peterloo—the 1819 massacre of peaceful reformers—hung over the debate. The government could not ignore the mass agitation for change. Peel accepted reform as the price of stability.

The 1832 Act set a precedent. In 1867, the franchise expanded again. In 1884, it expanded again. In 1918, women over thirty got the vote. The Great Reform Act did not create democracy, but it broke the aristocratic monopoly and established the principle that representation must eventually extend to all people. Every democratic expansion that followed traced its authority back to 1832, to the moment when Parliament finally acknowledged that the people had rights it could not forever deny.
